assets: main's history (DATA-repository) and the merge commits that carry each change
the commit plan and its Plan trailers, the proof of what each commit delivered
the push credentials of a cloud session
boundaries: a session's branch and the GitHub remote it pushes to
the pull request and the merge queue
a merge and the regeneration of the generated files it carries

threats.statement: A pull request claims a plan item, a lane or a review it did not deliver, so a merge looks justified by work or approval it does not carry.
A pushed history is rewritten or rebased, or several commits arrive in one push, so what lands is not what was judged commit by commit.

A merge of two branches leaves a generated file that matches neither generator run, or a change skips the local checks by pushing past the hook. Residual: the hook runs on the client, so a push that bypasses it is caught only by the gate, after the push.
A merge cannot be traced to its pull request, its commit plan and the verdict that let it in.

A secret in a commit is pushed to the public remote before the gate sees it. Residual: the pre-push scan is the only barrier before the push and runs on the client; a secret the gate finds is already public and must be rotated.
A head behind its base, or one that never merged its base, sits in the queue and keeps the changes behind it from landing. Residual: the merge queue's own capacity is GitHub's.

A session merges into main or deploys by hand, outside the merge queue. Residual: GitHub's ruleset, not this tree, is what refuses a direct push to main; .github/rulesets/main.json is the copy the owner applies, and no test reads back the ruleset GitHub enforces.
